Query feature: Degree of corruption: clean, light, heavy
Example: clean: "vector database comparison" | light: "vetor databse comparison" | heavy: "vctr dtbs cmprsn"
Why?: Meta-feature aggregating character/word-level corruption below. Clean → any mode works. Light → sparse breaks on corrupted tokens, dense subword tokenization partially robust. Heavy → both degrade, hybrid with fuzzy matching needed.

Query feature: Character level typos: insert / delete / substitute/ swap / keyword-adjacent
Example: "restrant" (delete), "resttaurant" (insert), "resyaurant" (keyboard-adjacent)
Why?: Character typos break exact token matching → sparse recall drops to zero for the corrupted term. Dense embeddings with subword tokenization are partially robust if enough of the subword survives. Signals a need to lean away from pure sparse.

Query feature: Word-level noise, dropped words, scrambled order, unnatural phrasing
Example: "database vector how setup" (scrambled), "best for search" (dropped key noun)
Why?: Scrambled order hurts dense models relying on position; dropped words hurt sparse recall. Both modes degrade, so hybrid may be most robust. Unnatural phrasing also means distribution mismatch for dense.

Query feature: Artifacts: encoding junks, truncation, copy-paste residue
Example: "how to fix â€™ encoding issue", "vector search perfx00ormance"
Why?: Artifacts introduce tokens in neither query intent nor corpus vocabulary — pure noise for both modes. Detection enables stripping before routing. If artifacts survive, sparse is especially hurt trying to match junk tokens.

Query feature: Corrupted identifiers, error codes in wrong places
Example: "error 0x80070005" pasted into a product search, "SKU-X4829Z" inside a natural language question
Why?: Structured identifiers in wrong context confuse routing: the identifier signals sparse but surrounding NL needs dense. Detecting this mismatch prevents the router from over-indexing on the structured token.

Example: mono: "wie funktioniert HNSW" | multi: "how does the Aufmerksamkeitsmechanismus work"
Why?: Cross-lingual terms break sparse entirely (German tokens won't match English index). Multilingual dense embeddings bridge the gap. Pure cross-lingual → strong dense signal. Code-switching → hybrid if some terms match the corpus language.

Example: "myocardial infarction prognosis" against a layperson corpus using "heart attack outcome"
Why?: The core sparse weakness measured directly. High mismatch → sparse fails to match relevant documents → dense needed. Low mismatch → sparse is safe and efficient. Arguably the single most important corpus-relative routing signal.

Example: "bank" (financial vs river), "jaguar" (animal vs car), "apple vision" (fruit vs tech)
Why?: Ambiguous queries retrieve mixed-intent results with both modes. Dense may cluster around the dominant sense, losing minority senses. Hybrid hedges: sparse catches lexical matches for both senses, dense biases toward the contextually likely one.

Example: broad: "machine learning" | narrow: "qdrant HNSW ef_construction tuning for 768-dim embeddings"
Why?: Broad queries match many documents — sparse returns too many, dense can rank semantically. Narrow queries need exact token matches — sparse precision dominates. Specificity determines whether the problem is ranking (dense) or matching (sparse).

Example: full: "what is HNSW?" against Qdrant docs | partial: "compare Qdrant vs Pinecone pricing" (only Qdrant side in corpus) | none: "tiramisu recipe" against a vector DB corpus
Why?: Unanswerable queries waste compute regardless of mode. Partial answerability benefits from hybrid (sparse catches answerable parts, dense finds related context). Detecting none early enables fallback instead of returning irrelevant results.
